scenes.heading: Configuration & Validation
scenes.narration: Real services don't hardcode config — they follow the twelve-factor rule and keep it in the environment. Let's load it with Viper and prove it's valid.

scenes.heading: The two bookends of input
items: Twelve-factor: config lives in the environment, not in code
Viper merges defaults, files, env vars, and flags
validator enforces that config and requests are actually valid
scenes.narration: Config and validation are the bookends of a service's input handling. Following twelve-factor, config that varies between deploys lives in the environment so one artifact runs everywhere. Viper is the de-facto loader that merges defaults, config files, environment variables, and flags into a single view. Then validator enforces that both your config and your request inputs are actually valid before the app trusts them.

scenes.heading: Config precedence order
scenes.narration: When the same key is set in several places, Viper resolves it by a fixed priority. An explicit Set beats everything, then flags, then environment variables, then the config file, and finally defaults, which lose to all. This order is intentional: it lets an operator override a file value with an env var in production without ever editing the image.

scenes.heading: Declarative validation with tags
scenes.narration: validator checks struct fields against validate tags — required, email, min, max, one-of — and returns a ValidationErrors listing every failure, not just the first. With a slice, the dive tag descends into each element so the rule after it applies per element. Here every tag element must be at least two characters. This is the gate that turns we parsed the input into the input is actually safe to use.

scenes.text: AutomaticEnv is not on by default, and dive with nothing after it does nothing.
scenes.narration: Two easy traps. Viper does not read environment variables until you call AutomaticEnv, so without it your exported vars are silently ignored. And the dive tag alone does nothing — it only tells the validator to descend, so you must follow it with a real rule like dive-comma-email to actually validate each element.

scenes.text: One typed Config, one shared validator — and Gin uses the same engine for request binding.
scenes.narration: So Unmarshal the merged view into one typed Config struct, share a single reusable validator instance, and validate at startup to fail fast. And remember Gin uses this exact validator engine under the hood, so a custom rule you register applies to every bound request too.
